paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.1:1 Rule 11.1 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.1. 1. Object of Process The essential ingredient … is that the process delivered to the defendant must be so delivered under circumstances which enable the court to conclude that [the defendant] knew, or reasonably should have known, what it was …Orazio v. Ciulla (1966), 57 W.W.R. 641 at 646 (B.C. S.C.). Master Marriott of the Ontario High Court of Justice quoted with approval Re Avery, [1952] 2 O.R. 192 (C.A.), at p. 199: Personal service has been said to be service made by delivering the process into the defendant's hands or by seeing him and bringing the process to his notice. Canadian Dominion Leasing Corp. v. Corpex Ltd.,[1963] 2 O.R. 497 at 498 (Master). And MacLeod J. of the Saskatchewan Court of Queen's Bench said: The object of the process is to give the defendant notice of the plaintiff's intention to bring the dispute before an impartial tribunal to hear the case on its merits. LaCoste v. Dee (1986), 53 Sask. R. 123 at 124 (Q.B.). In Al-Ghamdi v. Alberta, 2017 ABQB 169, 2017 CarswellAlta 393, Justice Hillier noted that “mere knowledge is not enough to constitute service.” His Lordship said: 7 As the Court of Appeal noted in Zahmol Properties Ltd. v. Calgary (City), 2012 ABCA 89 at para 7, leave to appeal ref'd [2012] SCCA No 235, mere knowledge is not enough to constitute service: • Service is a specialized form of notice. While “notice” is sometimes used as a synonym for “knowledge”, in this context notice encompasses the conveying of knowledge or information with intention to affect legal rights. • (Emphasis added) 8 See also Sandhu v MEG Place LP Investment Corp, 2012 ABCA 266 (at para 18): • In order to demonstrate proper service of the disallowances of the claims, it must be shown that the respondents received notice of the disallowances of their claims, in a context that made it clear that their rights were being engaged. • (Emphasis added)

paragraphs.heading: Part 11. Service Of Documents

sentences.text: Service not invalid

paragraphs.text: (1) This rule applies to service of (a) a document other than a commencement document, or (b) a document at the registered office of any person required by an enactment to have a registered office. (2) Service by mail or recorded mail is not invalid by reason only that (a) the addressee refuses to accept the mail, (b) the addressee returns the mail, (c) in the case of recorded mail, the addressee refuses to take delivery of the recorded mail, or (d) the addressee no longer resides or is otherwise not present at the address and has not provided the postal service with a current mailing address. Alta. Reg. 36/2020, s. 16

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.2:1 Rule 11.2 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.2. 1. Failure to Have Receipt Card Signed Service of the statement of claim on the defendant had not been effected in accordance with the Rules, in this case rule 22, since that is the method the plaintiff used. The acknowledgement of receipt card was not signed by the defendant. However, the purpose of service is to bring to the attention of a defendant the fact he is being sued. Obviously a defendant cannot defend an action against him if he does not know about it. If the Court is satisfied that the defendant, although not served as required by the Rules, is in fact aware of the action, that may be sufficient because the purpose of service is satisfied. In LaPierre v. Andrew (1983), 25 Alta. L.R. (2d) 308 (Q.B.), Shannon J., states at p. 312: “The principle that emerges from such cases is that a defective form of service can be deemed to be good and sufficient if it can be established that the document came to the attention of the party being served and as a consequence he acquired knowledge of the general nature of the claim being pressed against him.”Novak v. Dorcas (1986), 77 A.R. 233 at 235 (Master). 2. Failure to Effect Service a Mere Irregularity The court held that the failure to effect service is an irregularity which will support an application to set aside unless the defendant has delayed or acquiesced: Norman Wade Co. v. Yellowhead Machining Industries Ltd. (1983), 36 C.P.C. 185 (Master). A default judgment entered after one knows that the service permitted by the legislation was not effective is irregular, and if the irregularity has not been waived, the judgment may be set aside: Northside Electric v. Brynko Construction Ltd. (1976), 1 Alta. L.R. (2d) 157 (Dist. Ct.).

sentences.text: Agreement between parties

paragraphs.text: (1) If, in a contract that is the subject of an action, the parties agree on (a) a place for service, (b) a mode of service, or (c) a person on whom service may be effected, service of a document may be made in accordance with the agreement, and service is effected when so made. (2) An agreed method of service described in subrule (1) that applies outside Alberta must comply with rule 11.26. (3) An agreement about service of documents under this rule does not invalidate the service of a document that otherwise complies with the rules in this Part. Alta. Reg. 163/2010, s. 7

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.4:1 Rule 11.4 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.4. 1. No Immunity from Service Service may be effected upon a person who, but for the compulsion of legal process, would not otherwise be in Alberta. No immunity from service attaches to that person. This was the decision of Binder J. in G. (C.) v. L. (C.) (1996), 45 Alta. L.R. (3d) 309 (Q.B.), where at pp. 309–10, his Lordship said: … should a person who does not reside in Alberta, but is involved in litigation in Alberta and is required to attend in Alberta because of the litigation, be immune from service or execution of another exisiting or pending process because of the immunity enjoyed by such person beyond the jurisdiction of Alberta… Our Court of Appeal in the [Wilder v. 337236 Alberta Ltd. (1995), 38 Alta. L.R. (3d) 320] case has determined there is no immunity in the case of an outstanding warrant… … where does the Court draw the line? In other words, is it in the best interest of public policy, the administration of justice, and fundamental justice to adopt a concept of immunity with exceptions, or is the administration of justice, public policy, and fundamental justice better served absent such a concept? In my opinion, in the end it is the latter, as a matter of public policy that best meets the overall requirements of the administration of justice and fundamental justice. 2. Unconventional Forms of Service In Thompson v. Procrane, 2016 ABCA 71, 2016 CarswellAlta 430, an Originating Application was sent to the Respondent by e-mail. Was that sufficient service under the Rules? Justice Slatter, in determining whether to grant leave to appeal the order resulting from the hearing of the Originating Application, held that the service of the Originating Application was effective because it did actually come to the attention of the Respondent. His Lordship said, at paragraphs 11–13: 11 The applicant also notes that R. 11.4 requires that commencement documents be personally served. Rule 11.5 contemplates that service will be effected by leaving the document with the individual, or sending it by recorded mail. Service by email is not specifically contemplated for commencement documents. On the other hand, R. 11.27 enables the Court to validate service done “in a manner that is not specified by these rules if the Court is satisfied that the method of service used brought or was likely to have brought the document to the attention of the person to be served”. 12 Service is essentially a question of fact: did the person being served actually get a copy of the document? If the document was actually received, the method of service is inconsequential. The principle was stated in Sandhu v MEG Place LP Investment Corp., 2012 ABCA 266, 542 AR 12: 19 Service is a quintessentially practical consideration. The only point of service is that the defendant must get notice of the claim against it. Service is not some sort of magical or formalistic ritual that has to be followed. While civil procedure recognizes certain forms of service, unconventional forms of service that actually bring the legal process to the attention of the person being served are still effective. For example, assume that personal service is required, but when the process server arrives the defendant is not there. His wife agrees, however, to provide the documents to her husband when he returns. The next day the husband sends an e-mail, the contents of which make it clear that his wife did follow through, and that he is aware that he has been sued and served. This is effective service, even though it is unconventional. In this case, service of the Procrane Originating Application by email was an “unconventional form of service that actually brought the legal process to the attention of the person being served”. The use of an unconventional method does not mean that the service is automatically ineffective. 13 In this case Mr. Thompson fairly acknowledges that he did receive the Procrane Originating Application when he opened his email on the evening of November 23, 2015. At that moment he was “served”. Counsel for Procrane may have “taken a chance” by using an electronic method of service. It was possible that the Originating Application would not, in fact, come to Mr. Thompson's attention. It was also possible that Procrane might have had trouble proving service. However, in this case, Mr. Thompson did get the document, and he admitted that he got it. The service by email was perfectly valid. This ground of appeal is also of insufficient merit to warrant permission to appeal.

sentences.text: Service on individuals

paragraphs.text: (1) A commencement document may be served on an individual who is not required to be served by another method under this Division by (a) being left with the individual, or (b) being sent by recorded mail addressed to the individual. (2) Service is effected under this rule, (a) if the document is left with the individual, on the date it is left, or (b) if the document is sent by recorded mail, on the date acknowledgment of receipt is signed by the individual to whom it is addressed.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.5:1 Rule 11.5 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.5. Service of commencement documents by recorded mail In Al-Ghamdi v. Alberta, 2017 ABQB 169, 2017 CarswellAlta 393, Justice Hillier explained how service of commencement documents can be effected by use of recorded mail. His Lordship said: 56 Dr. Al-Ghamdi notes that commencement documents can be served by recorded mail, and that under r 11.2 service is not invalid simply because the addressee refused to accept the mail, that the addressee returns the mail, the addressee refuses to accept delivery of recorded mail, or the addressee is no longer at the address. 57 I note here that r 11.2 is a general provision, while r 11.5 is the more specific. R 11.5 expressly says that service of commencement documents by recorded mail is effected when the addressee acknowledges receipt. Therefore, the r 11.2 provisions cannot validate service that has not occurred as prescribed. 58 Dr. Al-Ghamdi also refers to the “presumption of service” provision in s 23 of the Interpretation Act. That section applies “if an enactment authorizes or requires a document to be sent, given, or served by mail” but expressly excludes “double registered or certified mail”. 59 Further, r 1.8(c) provides that s. 23 of the Interpretation Act does not apply to service of documents under the rules. 60 Finally, s 24 of the Interpretation Act (which is not excluded from application to the Rules of Court) says: A reference in an enactment to double registered mail, single registered mail, registered mail or certified mail includes any form of mail for which the addressee or a person on behalf of the addressee is required to acknowledge receipt of the mail by providing a signature. 61 Recorded mail is defined in the Appendix to the Rules of Court: “recorded mail” means a form of document delivery by mail or courier in which receipt of the document must be acknowledged in writing as specified in Part 11; (Emphasis added) 62 This definition is consistent with s. 24 of the Interpretation Act, RSA 2000, c I-8 since r 11.5 in Part 11 of the Rules of Court provides that service on an individual by recorded mail is effected by the signature of the addressee. Therefore, both the Rules of Court and the Interpretation Act provide that service by registered or recorded mail is effected when the addressee acknowledges receipt. The Interpretation Act further provides that a person may “sign on behalf of the addressee”, but the Rules of Court do not. I interpret that the more specific provision governs, and that therefore the Rules of Court do not permit acknowledgement by another person on behalf of the representee. 63 The Rules of Court have their own presumption for service by recorded mail—s. 11.22, but that section expressly excludes commencement documents. 64 I conclude that these provisions, read together, contemplate that service by recorded mail can only be effected by acknowledgement of receipt by the addressee. This does not mean, however, that service could not be validated by the court in the right circumstances in an application under r 11.27. As the Court of Appeal has said, service is a question of fact (Thompson v. Procrane Inc. (c.o.b. Sterling Crane), 2016 ABCA 71, at para 12) and not a “magical or formalistic ritual” (Sandhu, at para 19). Such an application is not before me, but I will consider whether service was effected in some other manner when exercising my discretion and considering the overall fairness of the circumstances.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.9:1 Rule 11.9 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.9. 1. Service upon Corporation's Registered Office See s. 256, Business Corporations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. B-9: 256. (1) A notice or document that is required or permitted to be sent to or served on a corporation may be (a) delivered to its registered office, or (b) sent by registered mail to (i) its registered office, or (ii) the post office box designated as its address for service by mail, as shown in the last notice filed under section 20. (2) Notwithstanding subsection (1), in the case of a notice of intent to dissolve a corporation, the notice may be sent by ordinary mail to the corporation addressedto its registered office, or (b) to the post office box designated as its address for service by mail, as shown in the last notice filed under section 20. (3) A notice or document sent by registered mail to the corporation in accordance with subsection (1)(b) or a notice sent by ordinary mail to the corporation in accordance with subsection (2) is deemed to be received or served at the time it would be delivered in the ordinary course of mail unless there are reasonable grounds for believing that the corporation did not receive the notice or document at that time or at all. See s. 22.3, Interpretation Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. I-8: 22.3. (1) If an enactment authorizes or requires a document to be sent, given or served by mail and the document is properly addressed and sent by prepaid mail other than double registered or certified mail, unless the contrary is proved the service shall be presumed to be effected (a) 7 days from the date of mailing if the document is mailed in Alberta to an address in Alberta, or (b) subject to clause (a), 14 days from the date of mailing if the document is mailed in Canada to an address in Canada. (2) Subsection (1) does not apply if (a) the document is returned to the sender other than by the addressee, or (b) the document was not received by the addressee, the proof of which lies on the addressee. These sections do not negate proper steps which may be taken by a plaintiff before the letter containing the statement of claim has been returned by the post office: Aero Aviation Centre (1981) Ltd. v. 210698 Investments Ltd. (1986), 45 Alta. L.R. (2d) 17 (Master). In Hvozdanski Estate v. Gasland Oil Ltd. (1999), 258 A.R. 358 (Master); affirmed (2000) 263 A.R. 399 (Q.B.), Master Funduk stated, at p. 359: Rules 14 and 15 apply to service of a statement of claim. Because a corporation is not a natural person service on the corporation has to be done differently than service on an individual, and rule 15(2) addresses that. Rule 15(2)(a) referentially incorporates the manner of service provided by statute if there is a manner of service provided by statute. In that case the Rules“as to mode of service” do not apply. That merely negates rule 15(1), which is incapable of application to a corporation anyway, and rule 15(2)(b). Rule 15(2)(a) does not negate the Rules as such, it merely negates the Rules“as to mode of service”. The failure of the personnel in the registered office (or those noted in R. 11.9(1)(a) to bring the matter to the attention of someone in authority does not render the service ineffectual: Black Gold Leasing Ltd. v. S & W Holdings Ltd. (1983), 42 A.R. 219 at 221 (Master). However, it is not enough to simply leave the notice at the registered office—it must be addressed to the company at the registered office. In 841656 Northwest Territories Ltd. v. Jodphur Holdings Ltd., [1992] N.W.T.R. 139 (C.A.), the court was dealing with a lease renewal notice which was left at the registered office of the landlord. The notice was addressed to the landlord's solicitors at their office (which was the registered office of the landlord). The letter was not passed on to the landlord in a timely fashion. Côté J.A. said at p. 140: In our view, a statutory registered office of a company is a place at which to serve the company, and it is not enough to serve the inhabitants of that place without addressing the notice to the company. To permit that would be an intolerable burden, especially where a number of companies share the same registered office, or where it is the premises of a busy law firm with many clients. A letter addressed to a law firm does not alert the firm to the fact that it is a notice which the firm must pass on at once to its client. It is argued in the alternative that here the law firm was the agent of the landlord, but it is admitted that the firm were not then the solicitors for the landlord in this matter. Again, the registered office of a company is a place, not a group of people. The notice of registered office does not appoint agents or give authority. Where an extra provincial company carries on business in Alberta but is not registered under the Alberta Business Corporations Act the court said: …Business Corporations Act does not contain any provision for service on a company which is carrying on business in Alberta, but which is not registered. There is no manner provided by statute as contemplated by Rule 15(2)(a), and it follows that service can be effected pursuant to Rule 15(2)(b), on an agent. Kroetsch v. H. W. Domnik Industries Ltd. (1985), 60 A.R. 69 at 71 (Master).

Application of Rule This rule only applies if an address for service is furnished: Calling Lake Resorts Ltd. v. Fonddulac Holdings Ltd. (Liquidator of) (1987), 49 Alta. L.R. (2d) 295 (Alta. C.A.); see also R. 26. 2. Obligation to Pick Up Mail from Address for Service In Wilson v. Bobbie (2006), 57 Alta. L.R. (4th) 342 (Q.B.), Slatter J. (as he then was) had before him an application to set aside a default judgment. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.16:1 Rule 11.16 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.16. “Accepting” versus “Admitting” Service This rule speaks of “accepting” service, not “admitting” service. The concepts are not the same. Rule 16(1) identifies an acceptance of service with the acceptance by a solicitor of a document by which an action or proceeding is commenced carrying with it an undertaking to file an appearance, or to appear, as the case may be. An admission of service, on the other hand, is merely an acknowledgement by a solicitor that a document has been served on him thereby obviating the necessity of an affidavit to verify service. I allude in this regard to R. 25. Harder v. Hayter,[1975] 4 W.W.R. 765 at 767 (Alta. C.A.). Therefore, use of the usual “service admitted” rubber stamp is not effective. An effective acceptance with the usual signature on behalf of the solicitor, should read: “Service of the within document is hereby accepted on (date) pursuant to R. 16(1) of the Rules of Court and an undertaking to file a statement of defence, demand of notice, or to appear, as the case may be, is hereby given.” The problem between “admitting” service and “accepting” service arose in Dynamic Oil Tools Inc. v. Dynamic Petroleum Services Inc. (2002), 6 Alta. L.R. (4th) 248 (Master). Master Alberstat said, at pp. 251–252: Rule 16 is a rule that deals with agency. That is, if a person appoints an agent to accept service of any document, that service is as effective as if the document was served on the principle. Kenneth Allison Ltd. (in liq) and Others v. A.E. Limehouse & Co. (a firm), [1990] 2 All E.R. 723; Montgomery, Jones & Co. v. Liebenthal & Co., [1898] 1 Q.B. 487. Rule 16 deals with serving an originating document as defined by our rules on a defendant's agent, his solicitor. To acknowledge that agency the solicitor must show his or her acceptance. In addition our rule 16 requires the solicitor to give an undertaking. The rule quite clearly says: “… and undertakes to file a statement of defence or demand of notice or undertakes to appear.” An acceptance of service without the undertaking is not sufficient. Both elements are required. There must be an acceptance and an undertaking to constitute good service. Kostiuk v. National Liberty Insurance Company of America (1934), [1935] 1 W.W.R. 106 (Sask. C.A.). In the present matter Mr. Smith “admitted” service. With this admission the clerks of the court allowed Mr. Pieschel to note the defendant in default. The question therefore also arises; is an admission of service the same or equivalent to an acceptance of service. The Shorter Oxford English Dictionary 3rd Edition defines the word accept as: “To accept service of a writ; to agree to consider it as validly served.” It defines the word admit as: “… to acknowledge, as lawful; to concede as true.” In my view these words are not alike. An admission of service is not an acceptance of service. Therefore the service in this matter is not good service. Even if the rule said “… accepts or admits…”, service in my opinion would not be good service. The second element, the undertaking to file a defence etc., is not clear and unequivocal in Mr. Smith's reply. His advise that he was “… awaiting their [his clients] instructions” is a clear indication that no agency relationship existed.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.17:1 Rule 11.17 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.17. 1. Sufficiency of Service … rule 24 says if an address for service is furnished it is sufficient to serve documents by leaving a true copy at that address; and in my view when a Notice of Motion names solicitors and gives the address of the law firm, that is giving an address for service. But in case I am wrong in that respect, rule 26 also says that all documents not required to be served personally upon the party affected thereby may be served upon his solicitor or his solicitor's agent. In this case, the Notice of Motion was signed “Odishaw and Odishaw per” Margaret Odishaw, and the backing sheet named Odishaw and Odishaw. In my view that was naming the firm of Odishaw and Odishaw as solicitor or solicitors for the appellant (or rather for the party who later became the appellant). Therefore, in my view rule 26 was also satisfied, and when the courier brought the document to Odishaw and Odishaw that was sufficient service on the solicitor for the party who then became the appellant a few days later. Bishop v. Bishop (1991), 113 A.R. 280 at 282-83 (C.A.). 2. When Deficient Service by single registered mail on a party's solicitor under R. 24 is deficient when no address for service has been furnished. When an address for service has not been furnished, service upon a solicitor is made by the solicitor admitting service, not by sending the document required to be served by registered mail. Calling Lake Resorts Ltd. v. Fonddulac Holdings Ltd. (Liquidator of) (1987), 49 Alta. L.R. (2d) 295 (C.A.), headnote. And Batten J. said: … it should be obvious that service on the solicitor can only be made after the filing and service of the demand for notice [i.e., only after the solicitor is on the record]. Russett v. Russett (1983), 27 Sask. R. 109 at 111 (Q.B.). 3. On Solicitor of Record If a solicitor is still formally on the record, then R. 26 can be used regardless of the fact that the party may have dismissed the lawyer. The neglecting to change a solicitor when he ceases to act does not discharge him … the solicitor on the record must be taken, as between him and the opposite party, to represent the client, unless the client not only discharges him but substitutes another solicitor on the record. Mackay v. J.D. Ross Construction Ltd. (1987), 36 D.L.R. (4th) 746 (N.S.C.A.), at 752–53, per Cotton L.J., quoting and applying Lady de la Pole v. Dick (1885), 29 Ch. D. 351 at 356–57. Failure of the solicitor's office staff to bring the document to the attention of the solicitor does not affect service. When counsel for the plaintiff pointed out that the formal judgment had been entered and had been served counsel for the Whissells said that he was not aware of that. He said that he did not have a “covering letter” indicating service. It is not the law that a document being served must have a “covering letter”. The formal judgment was served by leaving a copy of it at the office of counsel for Whissell. That is good service. If the receptionist or secretary does not give the document to her boss that is the boss' problem. It is not incumbent on the opposing counsel or the court to inquire into the “indoor management” of the counsel's office. Caisse Francalta Credit Union Ltd. v. W.C. Holdings Ltd. (1991), 116 A.R. 301 (Master), at 303, per Master Funduk. 4. Notice of Appeal The rule applies to serving a notice of appeal on the solicitor on record for the trial. In my view, a solicitor remains on the record until he is removed therefrom by the filing and service on him, and on the other parties in the proceedings … of a notice of change of solicitors or of a notice that the client desires to act in person; or until the solicitor files and serves on the client and on all other parties in the proceeding a notice of his intent to cease acting, supported by the filing of proof of service thereof …Harder v. Hayter[1975] 4 W.W.R. 765 at 768 (Alta. C.A.). 5. Role of lawyer of record when served In Tornqvist v. Shenner, 2024 ABCA 285, the Court set out the obligations of a lawyer of record when served with a document. Though the Court spoke specifically of contempt applications, the comments in paragraphs 26 and 27 have general application. The Court said: [26] The Rules permit service of both commencement and non-commencement documents on a lawyer of record: Rules 11.17 and 11.20(a).[3] In the ordinary course, the party serving the document, and the court, must be entitled to rely on the effectiveness of service on the lawyer of record, or the party’s stipulated address for service, as the case may be: Sandhu v MEG Place LP Investment Corporation, 2012 ABCA 266 at paras 21, 24, 25. As a corollary, there must be an obligation on the part of the lawyer of record to use reasonable steps to inform their client of documents received in that capacity. If lawyers of record could pick and choose which documents they pass along, Rule 11.17 would be meaningless and ineffective. [27] An obligation to bring an application to the attention of a client is consistent with the explicit duties of a lawyer of record set out in Rule 2.25(1) “:. (a) to conduct the action in a manner that furthers the purpose and intention of these rules:.” and “(b) to continue to act as lawyer of record while the lawyer is recorded in that capacity.” The obligation is also consistent with the fiduciary obligation of a lawyer to disclose material information to their client: Alice Woolley & Amy Salyzyn, Understanding Lawyers’ Ethics in Canada, 3rd ed (Toronto: LexisNexis, 2023) at 106. An application filed against the client is clearly material information: Recycling Worx Solutions Inc v Hunter, 2018 ABQB 395 at para 170; FIC Real Estate Fund Ltd v Lennie, 2014 ABQB 105 at para 63. [28] We see nothing in the Rules to distinguish a contempt application from any other application or commencement document in terms of the obligation of the lawyer of record who receives service. As set out above, a contempt application filed in an existing action for an alleged failure to comply with an order in that action is part of the same action, notwithstanding the distinguishing features of contempt proceedings. As such, absent an express distinction in the Rules, there is no principled basis to treat the obligation of the lawyer of record differently when served with a contempt application. [29] The appellant relies on Rule 10.52(2), which states “If a lawyer accepts service of a notice of an application seeking an order declaring the lawyer’s client to be in civil contempt of Court, the lawyer must notify the client of the notice as soon as practicable after being served.” According to the appellant, this Rule means that unless a lawyer accepts service of a contempt application, the lawyer is not obliged to notify the client. We do not accept the appellant’s interpretation of Rule 10.52(2). [30] The reference to accepting service in Rule 10.52(2) must be read in the context of the Rules as a whole, including those pertaining to service of commencement documents. Rule 11.16(1) states: “If a lawyer acts for a person in an action and the person must be served with a commencement document, the lawyer may, in writing, accept service on behalf of the person.” Rule 11.16 is distinct from Rule 11.17, which provides for service on a lawyer of record and does not include any reference to accepting service. A lawyer who “acts for a person in an action” will often, though not always, also be a lawyer of record for that person in the action. Rule 11.17 would be meaningless if service on lawyers of record pursuant to Rule 11.17 was only effective if the lawyer chose to accept service as contemplated in Rule 11.16. Accordingly, service may be effected on a lawyer of record pursuant to Rule 11.17 without any acceptance of service pursuant to Rule 11.16 or otherwise. [31] We do not accept that the reference to accepting service in Rule 10.52(2) should be interpreted as rendering Rule 11.17 inoperative in cases of contempt, as collapsing the distinction between Rules 11.16 and 11.17, or as negating duties inherent in the role of a lawyer of record. Rule 10.52(2) could be read as clarifying that a lawyer who accepts service pursuant to Rule 11.16 has a duty to notify their client akin to the duty inherent in the role of a lawyer of record.[4] It may serve other purposes. To decide this appeal, we need only confirm that Rule 10.52(2) does not mean that a lawyer of record may elect whether to accept service of a contempt application and whether to notify the client of any such application once received.

Rule 10.52(2) could be read as clarifying that a lawyer who accepts service pursuant to Rule 11.16 has a duty to notify their client akin to the duty inherent in the role of a lawyer of record.[4] It may serve other purposes.

To decide this appeal, we need only confirm that Rule 10.52(2) does not mean that a lawyer of record may elect whether to accept service of a contempt application and whether to notify the client of any such application once received.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.18:1 Rule 11.18 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.18. In Bank of Montreal v. Luciano, 2024 ABKB 314, Justice Marion discussed how to effect service on a self-represented litigant by the litigant accepting service of the document in writing. Justice Marion said: [26] However, one of the ways that service of commencement documents (and therefore also non-commencement documents under rule 11.20(a)) may be effected on self-represented litigants is if the self-represented litigant “accepts service of the document in writing”: rule 11.18(1); Powell Estate (Re), 2023 ABCA 311 at para 11; Toronto Dominion Bank v Halliday, 2022 ABKB 764 at para 12 [Halliday]. Service of a document may be proved to have been effected by an acknowledgment or acceptance of service in writing by the person served: rule 11.30(1)(b). If a self-represented litigant specifically acknowledges service in writing it is not necessary to obtain an order validating service: Powell Estate at para 16; Halliday at para 12(a). [27] Interpreting the rules together, there are two components to effect service in this manner on a self-represented litigant: (1) a written response from the self-represented party being served that (2) constitutes “acknowledgment or acceptance” of service. The assessment of these components is a question of fact having regard to all of the circumstances. [28] With respect to the writing requirement, electronic transmissions, including in the form of email, text messages, social media communications or a handwritten note may be sufficient if it is proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the communication was authored by the person being served: Halliday at para 12(a). [29] With respect to the “acknowledgment” or “acceptance” of service, this must be considered in the context of the meaning of “service”. Service is a specialized form of notice encompassing the conveying of knowledge or information with the intention to affect legal rights: Zahmol Properties Ltd v Calgary (City), 2012 ABCA 89 at paras 14-16; Sandhu v MEG Place LP Investment Corporation, 2012 ABCA 266 at para 18; R v Sharifi-Jamali, 2022 ABCA 114 at para 8. The purpose of service is to give a party notice: Post v Kellogg Brown & Root (Canada) Company, 2005 ABCA 390 at paras 5-6; at paras 11-12. Service is a question of fact: did the person being served actually get a copy of the document?: Thompson v Procrane Inc (Sterling Crane), 2016 ABCA 71 at para 12. [30] As per Sandhu at para 19: [19] Service is a quintessentially practical consideration. The only point of service is that the defendant must get notice of the claim against it. Service is not some sort of magical or formalistic ritual that has to be followed. While civil procedure recognizes certain forms of service, unconventional forms of service that actually bring the legal process to the attention of the person being served are still effective. For example, assume that personal service is required, but when the process server arrives the defendant is not there. His wife agrees, however, to provide the documents to her husband when he returns. The next day the husband sends an e-mail, the contents of which make it clear that his wife did follow through, and that he is aware that he has been sued and served. This is effective service, even though it is unconventional. [31] Accordingly, there are no formalistic or magical words that a self-represented person must use to be found to have accepted or acknowledged service. For example, the recipient does not need to use specific words of acceptance or acknowledgement. The crux of the question is whether the self-represented person has responded in writing that they received the document. [32] Therefore, if the evidence illustrates, on the balance of probabilities, that the self-represented person has, in writing, positively acknowledged, confirmed, accepted or verified that they actually received the document, this will usually be sufficient to establish service under rule 11.18(1) and, therefore, rule 11.20(a). [33] There may be unique circumstances where a written response from a self-represented litigant will be insufficient on its own to establish service, for example if the response indicates that the attached document was received but could not actually be opened, or perhaps if the recipient expressly states that they do not accept or acknowledge service in this manner (in which case an order validating service may be required). As noted, each case will depend on its facts.

paragraphs.text: 11.21. Service by electronic method
paragraphs.heading: Part 11. Service Of Documents

sentences.text: Service by electronic method

paragraphs.text: (1) A document, other than a commencement document, may be served by electronic method on a person who has specifically provided an address to which information or data in respect of an action may be transmitted, if the document is sent to the person at the specified address, and (a) the electronic agent receiving the document at that address receives the document in a form that is usable for subsequent reference, and (b) the sending electronic agent obtains or receives a confirmation that the transmission to the address of the person to be served was successfully completed. (2) Service is effected under subrule (1) when the sending electronic agent obtains or receives confirmation of the successfully completed transmission. (3) In this rule, “electronic” and “electronic agent” have the same meanings as they have in the Electronic Transactions Act. Alta. Reg. 163/2010, s. 8 1. Overview In Young v. Zukowski, 2024 ABKB 593, Justice Armstrong gave this explanation of how service by e-mail is to be properly effected: [33] Notwithstanding the existence of an Order for Substitutional Service, Mr. Young was at liberty to serve documents on Ms. Zukowski by another method of service permitted by the Rules of Court. Rule 11.21 allows for service of documents, other than commencement documents, by e-mail. Three conditions must be satisfied in order for service by e-mail to be properly completed: first, the party receiving service must have provided an address to which information in respect of an action may be transmitted; second, the information sent by e-mail must be received in a form that is usable for subsequent reference; and third, the party serving electronically must receive a confirmation that the transmission to the party being served was successfully completed. These confirmations are commonly called delivery or read receipts.

sentences.text: Additional service options in foreclosure actions

paragraphs.text: (1) In addition to the other methods of service described in this Part, service of every document in a foreclosure action, other than a commencement document, may be effected, unless the Court otherwise orders, (a) by leaving the document, addressed to the person to be served, at an address described in subrule (2), or (b) by sending the document by recorded mail, addressed to the person to be served, to an address described in subrule (2). paragraphs.text: 11.25. Real and substantial connection
paragraphs.heading: Part 11. Service Of Documents

sentences.text: Real and substantial connection

paragraphs.text: (1) A commencement document may be served outside Alberta and in Canada only if (a) a real and substantial connection exists between Alberta and the facts on which a claim in the action is based, and (b) the commencement document discloses the facts in support and specifically refers to the grounds for service of the document outside Alberta and in Canada. (2) A commencement document may be served outside Canada only if (a) a real and substantial connection exists between Alberta and the facts on which a claim in an action is based and the commencement document is accompanied with a document or affidavit that sets out the grounds for service of the document outside Canada, (b) the Court, on application supported by an affidavit satisfactory to the Court, permits service outside Canada, and (c) the person served with the commencement document is also served with a copy of the order permitting service outside Canada. (3) Without limiting the circumstances in which a real and substantial connection may exist between Alberta and the facts on which a claim in an action is based, in the following circumstances a real and substantial connection is presumed to exist: (a) the claim relates to land in Alberta; (b) the claim relates to a contract or alleged contract made, performed or breached in Alberta; (c) the claim is governed by the law of Alberta; (d) the claim relates to a tort committed in Alberta; (e) the claim relates to the enforcement of a security against property other than land by the sale, possession or recovery of the property in Alberta; (f) the claim relates to an injunction in which a person is to do or to refrain from doing something in Alberta; (g) the defendant is resident in Alberta; (h) the claim relates to the administration of an estate and the deceased died while ordinarily resident in Alberta; (i) the defendant, although outside Alberta, is a necessary or proper party to the action brought against another person who was served in Alberta; (j) the claim is brought against a trustee in relation to the carrying out of a trust in any of the following circumstances: (i) the trust assets include immovable or movable property in Alberta and the relief claimed is only as to that property; (ii) the trustee is ordinarily resident in Alberta; (iii) the administration of the trust is principally carried on in Alberta; (iv) by the express terms of a trust document, the trust is governed by the law of Alberta; (k) the action relates to a breach of an equitable duty in Alberta. (3) Without limiting the circumstances in which a real and substantial connection may exist between Alberta and the facts on which a claim in an action is based, in the following circumstances a real and substantial connection is presumed to exist:
(a) the claim relates to land in Alberta
(b) the claim relates to a contract or alleged contract made, performed or breached in Alberta
(c) the claim is governed by the law of Alberta
(d) the claim relates to a tort committed in Alberta
(e) the claim relates to the enforcement of a security against property other than land by the sale, possession or recovery of the property in Alberta
(f) the claim relates to an injunction in which a person is to do or to refrain from doing something in Alberta
(g) the defendant is resident in Alberta
(h) the claim relates to the administration of an estate and the deceased died while ordinarily resident in Alberta
(i) the defendant, although outside Alberta, is a necessary or proper party to the action brought against another person who was served in Alberta
(j) the claim is brought against a trustee in relation to the carrying out of a trust in any of the following circumstances:
(i) the trust assets include immovable or movable property in Alberta and the relief claimed is only as to that property
(ii) the trustee is ordinarily resident in Alberta
(iii) the administration of the trust is principally carried on in Alberta
(iv) by the express terms of a trust document, the trust is governed by the law of Alberta
(k) the action relates to a breach of an equitable duty in Alberta.
